pr.title: Make intrinsic fallback bodies cross-crate inlineable
pr.description:
This change was prompted by the stage1 compiler spending 4% of its time when compiling the polymorphic-recursion MIR opt test in `unlikely`.

Intrinsic fallback bodies like `unlikely` should always be inlined, it's very silly if they are not. To do this, we enable the fallback bodies to be cross-crate inlineable. Not that this matters for our workloads since the compiler never actually _uses_ the "fallback bodies", it just uses whatever was cfg(bootstrap)ped, so I've also added `#[inline]` to those.

See the comments for more information.

r? oli-obk
pr.author: Noratrieb

processing.reason: PR 121309 is a compiler inlining-policy optimization: it marks `#[rustc_intrinsic]` fallback bodies as cross-crate inlineable and prevents the MIR `Inline` pass from inlining those fallback bodies. The fallback bodies (e.g. `unlikely`, `likely`, `assume`) are semantically the intended definitions, and no ordinary-Rust caller/input distinguishes the old inlining policy from the new one by a concrete value. A real distinction would require reproducing rustc's intrinsic substitution/codegen behavior, which the fixed modern compiler and Miri do not expose here, especially for hint intrinsics such as `is_val_statically_known`. Encoding any differing return value or unrelated local-collapse would manufacture a difference not justified by the PR, so no valid source-grounded original/transformed pair can be validated.

analysis.originalLogic: Before this PR, the cross-crate inlinability query made only its pre-existing checks (e.g. instance kind and codegen/source annotations), with no special case for `rustc_intrinsic`, and the MIR `Inliner` had no rejection for intrinsic callees. Thus an intrinsic fallback body such as `unlikely` was treated like an ordinary function: it could be considered non-cross-crate-inlineable and left as an out-of-line call, while the MIR inliner could also attempt to inline its fallback body.
analysis.incorrectTransformation: The incorrect transformation is to leave a cross-crate call to a `rustc_intrinsic` fallback body as an ordinary out-of-line call (failing to make the fallback body cross-crate inlineable so the backend can inline it), and/or to let the MIR `Inline` pass inline that fallback body. The corrected behavior is: `cross_crate_inlinable` returns true for defs carrying `rustc_intrinsic`, while MIR `Inline` conservatively rejects such callees so codegen can use the real intrinsic implementation. For a two-program comparison, keep the same caller and intrinsic call, varying only whether the intrinsic fallback body is treated as ordinary/uninlineable versus cross-crate-inlineable-with-MIR-inline-rejection.
analysis.inputDomain: Rust compilation involving cross-crate calls to core intrinsic fallback bodies annotated with `#[rustc_intrinsic]`, such as `unlikely`, `likely`, `assume`, `is_val_statically_known`, `const_allocate`, and `const_deallocate`. Relevant inputs include optimized builds and MIR optimization tests (the description names the polymorphic-recursion MIR opt test using `unlikely`) and bootstrap builds where `#[cfg_attr(bootstrap, inline)]` is used instead of the non-bootstrap `rustc_intrinsic` path.
analysis.summary: Optimization PR: make intrinsic fallback bodies cross-crate inlineable so trivial fallbacks like `unlikely` can be inlined by codegen, while explicitly preventing the MIR Inline pass from inlining intrinsic fallback bodies because the MIR stage cannot know whether codegen implements the intrinsic better. Also adds bootstrap-only `#[inline]` attributes to the fallback definitions.
analysis.trigger: A call from one crate targets an intrinsic fallback body carrying the `rustc_intrinsic` attribute (for example `unlikely`), and the compiler evaluates cross-crate inlinability or runs the MIR Inline pass.
preconditions: The callee definition has the `rustc_intrinsic` attribute (or, under bootstrap, the corresponding fallback gets `#[inline]`).
The call crosses a crate boundary so cross-crate inlinability is relevant.
For the MIR-inline half of the change, the MIR Inline pass is considering an intrinsic fallback body as a callee.
The build is optimized enough for inlining decisions to matter.
pitfalls: Do not infer that making intrinsic fallback bodies cross-crate inlineable also authorizes the MIR Inline pass to inline them; the patch explicitly says MIR does not yet know whether codegen knows the intrinsic.
Place the `rustc_intrinsic` cross-crate-inlinable check before the later source-annotation match so intrinsic fallback bodies are not rejected by ordinary inline attributes.
Bootstrap and non-bootstrap configurations differ: `#[cfg_attr(bootstrap, inline)]` is added for the bootstrap path, while `#[cfg_attr(not(bootstrap), rustc_intrinsic)]` governs the normal path.
Do not claim the original slow behavior was reproduced or that any test was executed; no compiler was built and this patch contains no regression test changes.
analysis.testStrategy: Construct a cross-crate Rust case whose caller invokes an intrinsic fallback body such as `unlikely`, and check that codegen/backend inlining can inline the fallback rather than leaving an ordinary out-of-line call. Separately test the MIR Inline pass with a `rustc_intrinsic` callee and verify it is rejected/not inlined, even though the same def is cross-crate inlineable. The supplied patch adds no focused regression test, so such MIR-opt or codegen tests would be new coverage; assertions should inspect MIR or generated code rather than rely on execution of a built compiler here.
